title: Jeremiah 36:1–8
context: The narrator dates this word to the fourth year of Jehoiakim. The LORD commands Jeremiah to write on a scroll all the words he has spoken against Israel, Judah, and the nations since the days of Josiah, in the hope that the house of Judah will hear, turn from its evil way, and be forgiven (36:1–3). Jeremiah calls Baruch son of Neriah, who writes the LORD’s words from Jeremiah’s mouth (36:4). Jeremiah says he is “restricted” and cannot go into the LORD’s house, so he sends Baruch to read the scroll to the people on a fast day, hoping they will present their supplication and return (36:5–7); the text does not explain the restriction. Baruch does as Jeremiah commanded (36:8). Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: God’s word of judgment carries a purpose of mercy, and the faithful messenger carries it even when the prophet himself cannot.

verses.text: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: “In the fourth year of Jehoiakim… this word came to Jeremiah.” Arminian readers note the dating. The command to write the scroll comes at a particular moment in Judah’s history, during Jehoiakim’s reign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the historical setting. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as introducing the account of the scroll, and both see the writing down of the prophetic word as significant for its preservation.

verses.text: “Take a scroll of a book, and write in it all the words that I have spoken to you against Israel, against Judah, and against all the nations, from the day I spoke to you, from the days of Josiah even to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah is to write “all the words that I have spoken to you” since the days of Josiah. Arminian readers note that the spoken word is now to be written, so it can be read and heard again.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the writing of the prophetic word as part of God’s provision for his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing God’s word committed to writing, and neither builds a theory of the book’s composition on it.

verses.text: It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the evil which I intend to do to them, that they may each return from his evil way; that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin.”
verses.arminianNotes: “It may be that the house of Judah will hear… that I may forgive their iniquity.” Arminian readers stress the real hope of repentance. The scroll is written so that the people might turn and be forgiven.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm the sincere purpose of mercy in the word of judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that God announces judgment in order to call his people to return, and both see forgiveness as his desire.

verses.text: Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah; and Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all the LORD’s words, which he had spoken to him, on a scroll of a book.
verses.arminianNotes: Baruch wrote “from the mouth of Jeremiah all the LORD’s words.” Arminian readers note Baruch’s role as scribe. The words are the LORD’s, spoken through Jeremiah and recorded by Baruch.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the chain of transmission: the LORD, the prophet, the scribe. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing Baruch’s faithful service, and neither reads more into his role than the text states.

verses.text: Jeremiah commanded Baruch, saying, “I am restricted. I can’t go into the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah says, “I am restricted. I can’t go into the LORD’s house.” Arminian readers note that the text does not explain the restriction. Whatever its cause, the word is not hindered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise leave the reason unexplained. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the word goes out even when the prophet is restricted, and neither speculates beyond what the text says.

verses.text: Therefore you go, and read from the scroll which you have written from my mouth, the LORD’s words, in the ears of the people in the LORD’s house on the fast day. Also you shall read them in the ears of all Judah who come out of their cities.
verses.arminianNotes: Baruch is to read the scroll in the LORD’s house on the fast day. Arminian readers note the chosen occasion. A fast day, when people gathered to seek God, was a fitting time to hear his word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the fast day as an appropriate setting for hearing the call to repentance. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as placing the word before the gathered people at a time of seeking the LORD.

verses.text: It may be they will present their supplication before the LORD, and will each return from his evil way; for the LORD has pronounced great anger and wrath against this people.”
verses.arminianNotes: “It may be they will present their supplication before the LORD, and will each return.” Arminian readers note the repeated hope of repentance. The reading is meant to lead to prayer and turning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the purpose of the word as calling the people to seek God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as expressing a real hope that the people will return, joined to a sober warning of great anger and wrath.

verses.text: Baruch the son of Neriah did according to all that Jeremiah the prophet commanded him, reading in the book the LORD’s words in the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: “Baruch… did according to all that Jeremiah the prophet commanded him.” Arminian readers note Baruch’s faithful obedience. He carries out the task fully, even though it is risky.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise honor Baruch’s faithfulness. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an example of faithful service to the word, carried out by someone other than the prophet himself.
